always-all-in.tagline: Every hand. Every time. No exceptions.
always-all-in.behaviour: Shoves all 200 big blinds with any two cards.
story: always-all-in has exactly one move and makes it every hand from either seat, with any two cards. It never folds, never calls, never sees a flop it did not put its whole stack into.

It exists to be an oracle. Paired against a bot that only ever folds, the outcome of every hand is known in advance, which is what makes it useful for proving the betting engine and the chip accounting are right.

It is also the worst case for the equity code. Forcing an all-in before the flop every hand means enumerating 1,712,304 possible boards per new matchup, against 990 on the flop — roughly 1,700 times the work.

check-call.tagline: Never folds. Never raises. Never learns.
check-call.behaviour: Calls any bet, checks when checking is free.
story: check-call pays off every value bet ever made against it and never wins a pot it did not simply have the best hand in. It is the purest calling station that can exist.
Because it always sees every street a hand can reach, it is the opponent that exercises postflop play hardest — nothing ever ends early.

It also doubles as the cheapest correctness check in the project. Against always-all-in it scores exactly zero, to the chip, raw and adjusted. Neither bot looks at its cards, so the two halves of every duplicate pair are perfect mirror images and cancel completely. Any other number would mean a bug in the dealing, the pairing, or the accounting.

check-fold.tagline: Surrenders to any resistance at all.
check-fold.behaviour: Checks when free, folds to any bet.
story: check-fold never voluntarily puts a chip in the pot. If checking is free it checks; the moment anyone bets, it is gone.
It is the floor of the whole reference set and the first opponent any new bot should face, because the result is entirely predictable. It surrenders the big blind almost every hand it is dealt one.
Anything that cannot beat check-fold comfortably is either emitting illegal actions or folding hands it was being given for free.

random-randy.tagline: A coin flip with a random amount attached.
random-randy.behaviour: Picks uniformly among the legal actions, sizing at random.
story: random-randy chooses uniformly among whatever is legal. Facing a bet that is a clean third each to fold, call and raise; with no bet to face it is an even split between checking and raising. Raise sizes are uniform across the entire legal range, so it will min-raise and shove with equal enthusiasm.
Every choice is derived from the per-decision randomness the harness supplies and nothing else, which makes it perfectly reproducible: replay the same situation and it makes the same decision.

Its real job is reaching strange places. Scripted bots walk narrow paths; this one produces four-bet wars, tiny raises, short all-ins that fail to reopen the action, and every combination of streets — which is exactly what shakes out engine and logging bugs.

nit-all-in.tagline: Aces, kings, queens. Nothing else is worth opening for.
nit-all-in.behaviour: Shoves only AA, KK and QQ — 1.4% of hands.
story: nit-all-in waits for a premium pair and shoves it. Everything else goes in the bin: 18 of 1,326 combinations, one hand in seventy.

It is the folding extreme of the shove-or-fold family, and its results show exactly how expensive that is. Against always-all-in it wins the smallest margin of any bot in the set, because surrendering the blinds ninety-eight times out of a hundred bleeds away faster than the premiums bring back.

The interesting part is that its instinct is nearly right for one specific decision. Facing an all-in at this depth, the solved calling range is aces, kings, queens and ace-king suited — almost exactly this. nit-all-in is wrong as an opening range, not as a calling one.

better-all-in.tagline: Any ace, any king, any two big cards. Send it.
better-all-in.behaviour: Shoves pairs 99+, any two broadway, any ace, any king — 34.1%.
story: better-all-in shoves a third of all hands: every pocket pair from nines up, any two cards ten or higher, and — the clause that does most of the work — any ace or any king at all.
Those last two dominate the rest. The full ace and king rows mean it is shoving king-deuce offsuit and ace-trey offsuit, which makes it far looser than the word "premium" suggests.

It is also the most brutal bot in the set against pure aggression. A wide-but-selective range against a range of literally any two cards is an enormous edge, and it beats always-all-in by the largest margin anyone manages.

worse-all-in.tagline: Shoves the hands everyone else throws away.
worse-all-in.behaviour: Shoves only junk — offsuit, disconnected, no ace or king.
story: worse-all-in was built to be bad on purpose. Its range is the complement of everything worth playing: no pairs, nothing suited, no connectors or one-gappers, and no aces or kings. What survives is queen-nine offsuit down to seven-deuce offsuit.
That range averages 44% equity against a single random hand. It is committing two hundred big blinds as an underdog to any two cards, before the opponent even gets to fold the worst of theirs.

Its real value is as a controlled opposite of better-all-in. The two shove almost exactly as often — 32.6% against 34.1% — but over completely disjoint ranges. Aggression is held constant and only hand selection differs, so the gap between them measures selection alone.

solved-all-in.tagline: The best a shove-or-fold strategy can possibly do.
story: solved-all-in plays ranges computed rather than guessed — an approximate equilibrium of the game where both players may only shove or fold. Opening, it shoves 4.1% of hands. Facing an all-in it continues with aces, kings, queens and ace-king suited.
The odd inclusions are real, not noise. Ace-five and ace-four suited sit alongside ace-ten because wheel aces pick up straight equity and block an ace-heavy calling range.
Everything is tight because shoving risks two hundred big blinds to win one and a half. That needs either enormous equity or enormous fold equity, and at this depth neither is available often.

It tops the ratings, but the way it wins is the lesson. It beats better-all-in — yet better-all-in beats always-all-in by more than six times the margin solved-all-in manages against the same opponent. These ranges are the correct answer to an opponent playing the solved range; against one shoving every hand, folding 98% of the time declines a coin flip it should take. Unexploitable is not the same as maximally exploitative.

slp-fold.tagline: Bets what it has, calls with something, and never once bluffs.
slp-fold.behaviour: Value bets top pair, an overpair, over two pair, two pair made with both hole cards, or better; it continues passively with weaker pairs and draws.
story: Every bot in this family shares one postflop policy and one preflop chart. The policy is street-local: it sees the cards, the board, the money in front of it and the legal actions, and nothing about how the hand arrived there. It cannot tell a bet on a paired board from a bet on a wet one, and it has no memory of the street before. slp-fold is the honest one.

Top pair, an overpair, over two pair, two pair made with both hole cards, or better bets three quarters of the pot, or raises to three times a bet it is facing. A weak one-pair hand, under or middle two pair, or any draw calls. Board-only two pair is air. There is no randomness anywhere in it: replay the same spot a thousand times and it does the same thing a thousand times.

That makes it the control for the whole family. slp-bluff is this policy with air betting switched on, slp-balance is this policy with a mix; whatever those two win or lose against a given opponent is attributable to bluffing and nothing else. It also makes it perfectly readable — every chip it puts in means what it looks like, so anyone paying attention should never pay it off.

stats.label: Value
stats.value: Top pair, strong two pair, trips+

slp-bluff.tagline: The same policy, except every hand it misses is a bet.
slp-bluff.behaviour: Identical to slp-fold, but bets or raises one hundred percent of its air.
story: Every bot in this family shares one postflop policy and one preflop chart. The policy is street-local: it sees the cards, the board, the money in front of it and the legal actions, and nothing about how the hand arrived there. It cannot tell a bet on a paired board from a bet on a wet one, and it has no memory of the street before. slp-bluff is the aggressive pole of it.

Value hands play exactly as slp-fold plays them, and weak pairs and draws continue exactly the same way. The one changed line is the last one: where slp-fold checks and folds its air, slp-bluff bets three quarters of the pot with it, or raises to three times a bet. Every single time, with nothing at all.

Against anything that folds, this prints — and against anything that calls, it is the most expensive strategy in the set, because a bot that bluffs every miss is bluffing roughly two thirds of the time it sees a flop. The pair of it and slp-fold brackets the whole question the family exists to ask: what is bluffing worth, against this opponent, holding everything else fixed?

stats.label: Value
stats.value: Top pair, strong two pair, trips+

slp-balance.tagline: Mixes. Half its air bluffs, a third of its big hands trap, and a pair never raises.
slp-balance.behaviour: Bluffs half its air, traps with a third of trips-or-better, keeps strong two pair passive, and treats under or middle two pair like a weak pair.
story: Every bot in this family shares one postflop policy and one preflop chart. The policy is street-local: it sees the cards, the board, the money in front of it and the legal actions, and nothing about how the hand arrived there. It cannot tell a bet on a paired board from a bet on a wet one, and it has no memory of the street before. slp-balance is the one that mixes, and the three places it randomises are the whole strategy.

Half its air bets. Trips or better splits three ways to one: two thirds bet or raise, one third checks and calls instead, so the checking range is never only hands that gave up. Top pair and overpairs never re-raise. Over two pair and two pair made with both hole cards also check and call, while under and middle two pair behave like weak pairs: call an opening bet, but fold to a raise. Only a third of draws carry on against a raise.

Each mix is drawn from the per-decision randomness the harness supplies, so it is reproducible rather than genuinely random — the same spot always mixes the same way. It is the strongest street-local bot in the set, and it is still blind to the board, to the price, and to everything that happened on the street before.

slp-exploit-fold.tagline: Folds everything but an overpair to a bet, and bets everything that is not one.
slp-exploit-fold.behaviour: Facing a bet it continues only with an overpair or better; in an unbet pot it bets its value hands and all of its air.
story: Every bot in this family shares one postflop policy and one preflop chart. The policy is street-local: it sees the cards, the board, the money in front of it and the legal actions, and nothing about how the hand arrived there. It cannot tell a bet on a paired board from a bet on a wet one, and it has no memory of the street before. slp-exploit-fold is a counter-strategy rather than a strategy.

It is built around one observation: the rest of the family checks its weak hands and bets its strong ones, so a check is an admission. In an unbet pot it bets — value hands for value, air as a bluff, both three quarters of the pot. Facing a bet it does the opposite and folds everything short of an overpair, including top pair, including every draw.

That asymmetry is the exploit and also the hole. It gives up far too much to anyone willing to bet into it, which is precisely why slp-balance now mixes a third of its big hands into its checking range: a checking range that is not capped takes the whole exploit away.

slp-exploit-solved.tagline: Min-raises the button with any two cards, then plays slp-exploit-fold.
slp-exploit-solved.behaviour: Opens every unopened button to the minimum with any two cards, defers to the solved push-fold table facing an all-in, and uses the slp-exploit-fold policy after the flop.
story: Preflop it throws the chart away on the button. First in, with any two cards, it raises to the legal minimum — one hundred percent of hands, for the cheapest price the rules allow. The one preflop spot it takes seriously is an all-in: facing one it consults the same solved push-fold table solved-all-in uses, calling with aces only from the button and with the solved range out of the big blind.
After the flop it is slp-exploit-fold exactly — bet the unbet pot with anything, fold everything but an overpair to a bet.

The min-raise open is the interesting failure. Raising the bottom of the range for the minimum builds a pot with hands that cannot continue, and it is the only bot in this family that loses money to always-all-in, which every other street-local bot beats comfortably. Being cheap to enter a pot is not the same as being free.

nitty-nancy.tagline: Opens only TT+, AT+ and KQ, and folds to a 3-bet without QQ+ or AK.
nitty-nancy.behaviour: Opens only TT+, AT+ and KQ, and folds to a 3-bet without QQ+ or AK.
story: nitty-nancy plays a tiny range and plays it straightforwardly. It opens tens or better, ace-ten or better, and king-queen — everything else goes in the bin before the flop.
Facing a 3-bet it continues with queens, kings, aces and ace-king only, and it re-raises those rather than calling. There is no flatting range and no bluff.

After the flop it never bluffs at all: it value bets top pair or better, calls a bet only with top pair or better, and re-raises only with a straight or better. Every chip it puts in means exactly what it looks like.

calling-station.tagline: Calls any preflop size inside the opening chart, and any postflop bet or raise with a pair or a draw.
calling-station.behaviour: Calls any preflop size inside the opening chart, and any postflop bet or raise with a pair or a draw.
story: calling-station never folds to a number. If a hand is in the small-blind opening range it calls, whether the raise is two big blinds or eighty.

After the flop, any pair at all is enough to call — bottom pair with no kicker included — and so is any draw, at any price, including a raise of its own bet. With less than that it falls back on the default balanced policy.
It is the archetype everyone recognises: the player you cannot bluff, and cannot fold out, and therefore should never bluff at.

stats.label: Postflop
stats.value: Calls with any pair or draw

passive-patty.tagline: Turns every raise into a call, and folds anything below top pair.
passive-patty.behaviour: Turns every raise into a call, and folds anything below top pair.
story: passive-patty uses the same chart as everyone else, then downgrades every raise in it to a call. It never takes the betting lead preflop.
After the flop it calls with top pair or better and folds everything worse. It will not bet, will not raise, and will not bluff.
The single exception is quads: only four of a kind is enough to make it put in a raise. Everything short of that gets called down or thrown away.

chasing-charlie.tagline: Calls any suited hand preflop and any draw at any price.
chasing-charlie.behaviour: Calls any suited hand preflop and any draw at any price.
story: chasing-charlie has heard that suited cards are good and that draws are worth chasing, and it has taken both lessons further than intended.
Preflop it calls with any two suited cards, up to a medium raise — it will not stack off cold, but almost nothing else gets it to fold.

After the flop, a draw is a call regardless of price. A gutshot facing a pot-sized bet gets exactly the same treatment as a flush draw facing a third of the pot. It never checks whether the odds are there.

semi-bluff-sarah.tagline: Raises every draw and folds every other unpaired hand.
semi-bluff-sarah.behaviour: Raises every draw and folds every other unpaired hand.
story: semi-bluff-sarah has learned that draws play better as raises than as calls, and applies it without exception. Every flush draw, every open-ender, every gutshot goes in as a raise — three times the bet when facing one, three-quarters pot when checked to.
The other half of the rule is just as absolute: any hand that is neither a pair nor a draw is folded immediately. It has no pure bluffs and no float.
The result is maximum fold equity and almost no showdown value, which makes it a nightmare for passive bots and food for anyone willing to re-raise.

trapping-thomas.tagline: Slow-plays premiums and good postflop hands until the river.
trapping-thomas.behaviour: Limps or calls with QQ+, AK, check-calls good hands through the turn, then takes aggressive river action.
story: trapping-thomas starts the slow-play before the flop: with aces, kings, queens or ace-king it only limps or calls, while every other hand stays on the shared chart.

With top pair or better on the flop and turn it checks back in position and check-calls out of position. On the river it finally releases the trap: check-raising four times out of position, or making a normal value bet or raise in position.
It never bluffs, so every river raise is genuine. The earlier streets keep opponents in, but checking behind can still cost it value when nobody takes the bait.

triple-barrel-travis.tagline: As preflop raiser, bets all three streets regardless of its cards.
triple-barrel-travis.behaviour: As preflop raiser, bets all three streets regardless of its cards.
story: triple-barrel-travis raises preflop like everyone else. From there, if it was the last raiser, it bets the flop, the turn and the river — with the nuts, with air, with anything.
It does not check whether the board helped it, whether it improved, or whether the opponent has shown strength by calling twice. The plan was made before the flop.
Facing a re-raise it reverts to the default policy, which is the only brake in the whole strategy.

one-and-done.tagline: C-bets the flop as preflop raiser, then gives up on every later street.
one-and-done.behaviour: C-bets the flop as preflop raiser, then gives up on every later street.
story: The mirror image of triple-barrel-travis, and the more common human leak. one-and-done fires a continuation bet at every flop it raised before, then stops.
On the turn and river, without a pair or a draw, it simply checks and folds. The c-bet was automatic; so is the surrender.
It is the cheapest bot in the set to exploit — call the flop with anything and take the pot away on the turn.

scared-sam.tagline: Tightens at 25 big blinds and panics completely at 50.
scared-sam.behaviour: Folds one-pair hands to a 25 bb wager, requires a straight at 50 bb, and stops raising as pots grow.
story: scared-sam plays the baseline until the chips start looking like real money. Once a preflop pot reaches twenty-five big blinds it stops raising and only calls.

After the flop, a wager of twenty-five big blinds folds every one-pair hand; only strong two pair or better continues. At fifty big blinds the requirement jumps again to a straight or better, so even a set goes in the muck.

It also stops raising once the whole postflop pot reaches fifty big blinds. The thresholds are absolute rather than pot-relative, mimicking a live player who reacts to the amount of money instead of the price being offered.

tilted-terry.tagline: Calls any open with anything, bluffs all air, folds only to a re-raise.
tilted-terry.behaviour: Calls any open with anything, bluffs all air, folds only to a re-raise.
story: tilted-terry calls preflop opens with any two cards. Position, price and holding are all irrelevant; only a re-raise gets through to it.
After the flop, any pair is a call and every airball is a bluff. It bets when checked to and raises when bet into.
The one thing that stops it is a second raise on the same street. Faced with that, the air finally goes in the muck — usually several streets too late.

min-raise-miranda.tagline: Plays the default strategy but every raise is the legal minimum.
min-raise-miranda.behaviour: Plays the default strategy but every raise is the legal minimum.
story: min-raise-miranda makes exactly the same decisions as the baseline strategy. Fold where it folds, call where it calls, raise where it raises.
The only difference is the number. Every raise is the smallest one the rules permit — the nuts and a bluff are both raised to the minimum.
Nobody is ever priced out and no pot ever grows. It is a controlled experiment in what bet sizing alone is worth.

overbet-oliver.tagline: Plays the default strategy but every raise is twice the pot.
overbet-oliver.behaviour: Plays the default strategy but every raise is twice the pot.
story: overbet-oliver is min-raise-miranda's opposite and its control. Identical decisions, one changed number: every raise is two times the pot.
There are no small bets in its game. A thin value bet and a total bluff both arrive as an overbet.
Together the two isolate bet sizing from hand selection: same strategy, same spots, opposite extremes of aggression in chips.

aggressive-andy.tagline: Raises every hand once, then bets every pot nobody has bet into.
aggressive-andy.behaviour: Opens any two cards for a small raise, bets any pair and all the air it has a story for, and only steps down when someone bets into it.
story: aggressive-andy raises any two cards when it can open the pot or isolate a limp, but always for a small size — two big blinds, never more. If it faces an existing raise, it skips the automatic aggression and plays straight off the chart.

After the flop the rule is almost as short. In an unbet pot it bets: with any pair at all, with air whenever it is last to act and has been checked to, and with air out of position whenever it was the one who raised before the flop. Three quarters of the pot, every time.

The single thing that stops it is a bet. The moment chips come the other way it drops the act entirely and reverts to the default balanced policy, which folds the air it was firing with a second earlier. It is not fearless — it is only relentless while nobody pushes back.

slp-odds.tagline: Scores its hand against the board, and its draws against the price.
slp-odds.behaviour: slp-balance plus three things: a hand is worth what it is worth on this board, a draw continues only when the odds cover the call, and a raise of its own bet is not treated like an opening bet.
story: Every bot before this one values a hand by its class. Top pair is top pair, whether the board is king-seven-deuce rainbow or four to a flush. slp-odds scores the hand instead: it starts from the class, subtracts what the board threatens, and lands on a number out of a hundred. That number falls into one of five bands, and the band picks the action -- nutted raises, strong calls, medium and marginal continue only at a price that makes sense, and air is left to the old bluffing rule.

The same top pair is worth 44 points on a rainbow board and 24 with four to a flush out there. It goes from a hand that raises to a hand that folds to a real bet, without a single rule mentioning top pair.

Draws stop being one bucket. Outs are counted, turned into equity at four percent each on the flop and two on the turn, and compared against what the call costs as a share of the pot it would build. A flush draw calls a third of the pot and folds to four times it; a gutshot folds to both.

It is also the first bot that notices being raised. A raise of its own bet is a far stronger range than an opening bet, so facing one the two value bands ask for more points -- a dry set stops being a raising hand and becomes a calling one, an overpair stops being a calling hand and starts needing a price. Even then one re-raise in three is flatted instead, and one bet in five is raised with nothing made -- a re-raise included, which needs a bluff to have been raised in the first place and so happens about once in twenty-five. Neither its raising range nor its calling range is only ever what it looks like. Nothing here reads the action history, so this is still a street-local policy -- most of what the earlier bots were missing was arithmetic, not memory.

the-crusher.tagline: The first one that asks what you have.
the-crusher.behaviour: Scores the opponent's line on the same scale it scores its own hand, acts on the difference, and sizes its bets to get the stacks in.
story: Every bot before this one scores its own hand and stops. the-crusher scores the opponent's line too -- out of a hundred, on the same scale -- from what they have actually done. Checking is 20 and calling 34; betting is 46 and raising our bet 68; a second raise is 76 and a third 82. A big bet claims more than a small one, two thirds of the pot being the size that moves nothing. And the preflop pot type moves it most of all, because those are not neighbouring strengths: an opening range is most of a deck, a three-bet is a tenth of it, a four-bet is the top few percent and a five-bet is aces and kings. A limped pot is worth ten less, a single open six less -- an opening range is still most of a deck -- a three-bet fourteen more, a four-bet twenty-six, a five-bet thirty-four. And a continuation bet, the preflop raiser's first bet on the flop, claims twelve less than any other bet, because it is made with the whole range that raised, hit or not. The same two-thirds-pot bet reads 36 in a limped pot and 88 in a four-bet one.

One more term is about the board rather than the action. Raising before the flop is what separates two ranges: the raiser keeps the aces, kings and broadway cards, and the caller, by declining to raise, mostly does not. So a king-jack-deuce flop belongs to whoever raised and a seven-five-trey flop belongs to whoever called, and the score moves nine points toward them either way. In a limped pot nobody raised, nothing separates the ranges, and the term is zero; past a three-bet both ranges are made of big cards, so the swing halves -- a low board does not belong to a caller who is still holding four-betting hands. The same bet on the same street reads 59 on the first board and 41 on the second.

The second half is sizing, and it is a separate question from whether to put chips in at all. Every intent has two candidate sizes rather than one, because one size is readable and two are not, and which of the two gets used is a weighted draw. The pair depends on whether we are raising a raise and on how polarised the opponent's range is -- a different question from how strong it is. A polarised range is nuts or nothing, with no medium hands in the middle to punish, so bluffing it big burns money and value betting it big does not: half the pot or a quarter over it, at three to one. A merged range is full of medium hands, so the pair inverts to a third and two thirds.

Polarisation is read off the bet size and the board. Nobody bets the pot with a medium hand and nobody bets a fifth of it with the nuts. A board where the obvious draw has arrived, and a board so dry that almost nothing connects with it, both split a betting range in two; a wet, connected, undrawn board does the opposite, because it is full of pairs and draws worth betting. Four-bet ranges are uniformly strong and so are merged rather than split, and a range that has only checked is capped, not polarised.

Then the board, our own outs, their range and the geometric plan all move the weight rather than the size. Live draws out there add twelve points to the big side and a bone-dry board takes twelve away; a paired board takes eight, since it hands out fewer second-best hands to get paid by; a bluff with real outs adds ten, because it still has a hand when it is called; a bluff into a range that has shown nothing loses ten, because the small size folds out the same hands. The size that would get the stacks in no longer dictates anything -- it pulls fifteen points toward whichever of the two candidates it lands nearer, and needs no cap of its own any more, because nothing bets that number.

The second half is sizing. A fixed fraction of the pot cannot get two hundred big blinds in by the river, so when the edge is big enough to want stacks the bet is the geometric one: the fraction that, repeated on every street left, ends exactly all in. Two hundred blinds deep that is three pot-sized bets; in a shallow pot it is a twentieth of the pot. Nothing else in the project has ever planned past the street it was on.

One thing does not follow from the edge, and gets read straight off the opponent's score: how often to bluff. A range that has shown nothing is bluffed at one time in three, a range that has raised twice one time in eight. And one correction the edge cannot make on its own -- it cannot tell holding a hand from neither player holding anything -- so checking down and bluff-catching both require a hand that could actually win a showdown, and everything below that falls through to the bluff.

The sizes are chosen to overlap. A quarter over the pot is both a value bet against a polarised range and a bluff against a merged one; half the pot is a value bet, a thin one and a bluff; two and a half times the pot is a value re-raise and a bluff re-raise. Reading the hand off the size is meant to be impossible, which is the point of having two of them.

The code is split the way the questions are. What our hand is worth, what their line claims, whether that is enough to raise, whether it is enough to call, and how much to put in are five files, and folding is none of them -- it is what is left when nothing else says yes. Keeping the last one apart from the rest is the whole reason the same holding can arrive as two different sizes.

tables.title: How polarised their range is
tables.note: Starts at 50 and counts as polarised at 55. A different question from how strong the range is: this one decides the sizing, not the action.

tables.title: When to raise, when to call
tables.note: A bluff-catch also needs a hand worth 14 points or more, and a price no higher than 42 minus a third of their claim -- so nearly half the pot against a range that has only checked, and a tenth against one that has raised twice. Only hands under 14 points bluff.

tables.title: Two sizes for everything
tables.note: Every size is reachable at least two ways, so the number on its own gives nothing away: a quarter over the pot is a value bet against a polarised range and a bluff against a merged one.

tables.title: What moves the odds
tables.note: Clamped between 5 and 95 percent. The geometric size -- the fraction that, repeated each street, ends exactly all in -- no longer picks a number, it only leans the choice between the two.
rows: Bluffing with eight outs or more

tables.title: What a bet costs, and the outs that cover it
tables.note: Price is the share of the pot the call would build, not of the pot as it stands. Outs are worth four percent each on the flop and two on the turn.

tables.title: Frequencies
tables.note: How often to bluff does not follow from the edge, so it is read straight off their strength. Bluff frequency and bet size draw from different slices of the per-decision randomness, so whether it bluffs and how big are uncorrelated.
